problem: Write a function solve(text) that performs run-length encoding on a string. The result should be a string where each run of identical consecutive characters is replaced by the character followed by the run length. The encoding must preserve the original order of runs. For an empty string, return an empty string. For example, solve('aaabbc') should return 'a3b2c1'. The function signature is solve(text: str) -> str. The input is always a valid string (possibly empty).
title: Run-Length Encoding with Empty String Guard

problem: Write a function solve(s) that takes a string s containing only the characters '(', ')', '[', ']', '{', '}' and determines whether the brackets are balanced. A string is balanced if: every opening bracket has a corresponding closing bracket of the same type, brackets are closed in the correct order (proper nesting), and no closing bracket appears without a matching opening bracket. Return True if balanced, False otherwise. The empty string is considered balanced. The function must process the entire string and return a boolean.
title: Balanced Brackets with Nesting Depth

problem: Write a function solve(items) that takes a list of integers and returns a new list containing only the unique elements from the original list, preserving the order of their first appearance. The function should handle empty lists and lists with all duplicate elements. The return type is a list of integers. For example, solve([3, 1, 3, 2, 1]) should return [3, 1, 2].
title: Stable Unique Elements

problem: Write a function solve(intervals) that takes a list of intervals, where each interval is a pair [start, end] of integers with start <= end. Intervals are closed, meaning [1, 2] and [2, 3] overlap at 2 and should be merged. Return a new list of merged intervals sorted in ascending order by start; if two starts are equal, the one with the smaller end comes first in the input processing order; however, after merging, intervals will be disjoint. The input list may be empty. Do not modify the input list. The return type is a list of two-element lists of integers. Example: solve([[1,3],[2,6],[8,10],[15,18]]) returns [[1,6],[8,10],[15,18]]. solve([[1,4],[4,5]]) returns [[1,5]]. solve([[5,7],[1,3]]) returns [[1,3],[5,7]].
title: Merge Overlapping Closed Intervals

problem: Given a string s, return the length of the longest substring that contains no repeated characters. If s is empty, return 0. The signature is solve(s: str) -> int. The substring must be contiguous. All characters are ASCII. If multiple substrings have the same maximum length, any one of them may be considered; only the length is returned.
title: Longest Distinct Run

problem: Write a function solve(n) that returns the prime factorization of n as a list of [prime, exponent] pairs, sorted by prime in ascending order. The input n is an integer from 1 to 1000000 inclusive. Each prime and exponent must be an integer. Return an empty list when n is 1.
title: Prime Factor Counts

args: a A b B c C
apple banana apple Cherry banana apple
x y z x y x
One two TWO three Three THREE four

problem: Write a function solve(text) that returns a list of [word, count] pairs sorted by count descending, then by word ascending. Words are compared case-insensitively and counted case-insensitively. A word is any maximal sequence of ASCII letters (a-z, A-Z) and digits (0-9). Words that differ only in case are the same word; the output word should be lowercase. If text is empty or contains no words, return an empty list. The input is a string.
title: Case-Insensitive Word Histogram

problem: Write a function solve(matrix) that returns the transpose of a 2D matrix. The input matrix is a list of lists, where each inner list represents a row. All rows have the same length. If the matrix is empty (i.e., []), return []. If the matrix has rows but no columns (e.g., [[]] or [[], []]), return an empty list. The output should be a new matrix where the element at row i, column j is the element at row j, column i of the input. The function signature is: solve(matrix) -> list. The input matrix may contain integers, strings, booleans, or lists (but not nested lists as elements). Order is preserved as per the transpose definition; no tie-breaking is needed.
title: Transpose a Matrix

problem: Write a function solve(nums) that takes a list of integers (which may include negative numbers, zero, duplicates, and positive numbers) and returns the smallest positive integer (greater than 0) that does not appear in the list. The function must return an integer. If the list is empty or contains no positive integers, return 1. The input list is not guaranteed to be sorted. Duplicates and negative numbers should be ignored. The solution should be efficient (O(n) time and O(1) extra space is ideal, but O(n) space is acceptable for this exercise).
title: First Missing Positive Integer in a List

problem:
Write a function solve(items, offset) that returns a new list containing the elements of items rotated by the signed integer offset.

Signature: solve(items: list, offset: int) -> list

Rules:
- A positive offset moves elements to the right: offset=1 turns [1,2,3] into [3,1,2].
- A negative offset moves elements to the left: offset=-1 turns [1,2,3] into [2,3,1].
- Offset is allowed to be any integer; reduce it modulo the length of the list.
- If items is empty, return a new empty list regardless of offset.
- Return a new list; do not modify the input list.
- Preserve the original order of the remaining elements.

Examples (not test cases): offset equal to the list length returns a copy of the original order; offset 0 also returns a copy.
title: Rotate a List with Signed Offsets

problem: Given a list of half-open intervals [start, end) represented as tuples (start, end), where start and end are integers and start < end, return the maximum number of intervals that overlap at any point, i.e., the peak concurrency. Two intervals overlap if they share at least one point. Since intervals are half-open, an interval ending at time t does not overlap with one starting at time t. If the input list is empty, return 0. The solve function signature is: def solve(intervals: list[tuple[int, int]]) -> int. Ordering and tie-breaking do not affect the result; only the maximum count matters.
title: Peak Half-Open Intervals

problem: Write a function solve(items) that flattens a nested list structure exactly two levels deep. The input items is a list where each element is either an integer or a list of integers. Return a new flat list of integers in the order they appear, preserving the left-to-right order within and across sublists. Do not flatten deeper structures; if a sublist contains a list, that inner list should be included as an element (but this will not occur in the given cases). Empty sublists contribute nothing. The input list may be empty, in which case return an empty list. The return type is a list of integers.
title: Flatten Nested Lists Two Levels Deep

args: A man, a plan, a canal: Panama

problem: Define solve(s: str) -> bool that returns True if the string s becomes a palindrome after removing all characters except letters and digits, ignoring case. The filtered string is formed by keeping only alphanumeric characters (a-z, A-Z, 0-9) and converting them to lowercase. Return True if the filtered string reads the same forwards and backwards, including when it is empty or has one character. Characters outside ASCII letters and digits are removed. This function has no side effects.
title: Palindrome After Filtering Digits

problem: Write a function solve(nums, target) that returns the number of index pairs (i, j) with i < j such that nums[i] + nums[j] == target. The input nums is a list of integers and target is an integer. Return an integer count. Edge cases include an empty list, a single-element list, and duplicate values. The order of pairs does not matter, but the count must include all valid index pairs.
title: Count Index Pairs with a Given Sum

problem: Write a function solve(grid, start, end) that returns the length of the shortest path from start to end on a 2D grid. The grid is a list of strings, where '.' is an open cell and '#' is a wall. start and end are tuples (row, col) with 0-based indexing. Movement is allowed in the four cardinal directions (up, down, left, right). The path length is the number of steps (edges) from start to end. If no path exists, return -1. If start equals end, return 0. The grid is rectangular (all rows have the same length). start and end are guaranteed to be within bounds, but may be on walls (in which case return -1, unless start==end? Actually if start==end and on a wall, still return 0? The problem says if start equals end, return 0, regardless of wall? Let's define: if start == end, return 0 (even if wall). Otherwise, if start or end is a wall, return -1. Return type is int.
title: Shortest Path on a Unweighted Grid

problem: Write a function solve(items) that takes a list of strings and returns a list of the distinct strings ranked by frequency (most frequent first), breaking ties by the string's natural ascending lexicographic order (case-sensitive). The returned list should contain only the strings, not their counts. If items is empty, return an empty list. The input list may contain duplicate strings; each distinct string appears exactly once in the output. Example: solve(["apple", "banana", "apple", "cherry", "banana"]) should return ["apple", "banana", "cherry"] because apple and banana appear twice (apple < banana alphabetically) and cherry appears once.
title: Fully Ordered Frequency Ranking

problem: Write a function solve(intervals) that takes a list of integer pairs [start, end] where start <= end, and returns a list of merged, non-overlapping intervals sorted in ascending order by start, then by end. Two intervals [a, b] and [c, d] overlap or touch if c <= b (assuming a <= c). When merging, the new interval is [min(a, c), max(b, d)]. The input may be empty. The output must be a list of lists, each with exactly two integers. Ordering: intervals sorted by start ascending, then end ascending. Edge conditions: intervals that only touch (e.g., [1,2] and [2,3]) are merged into [1,3]. Intervals are inclusive. For an empty list, return an empty list.
title: Merge Integer Intervals

problem: Write a function solve(records, city, min_age) that filters a list of short records. Each record is a dict with keys 'name' (str), 'age' (int), and 'city' (str). Return a list of names (str) for records where the city matches exactly (case-sensitive) and age >= min_age. The result must be sorted by age descending, then by name ascending (case-sensitive). If multiple records have the same name, age, and city, include the name once per matching record (duplicates preserved). If records is empty, return []. If no records match, return []. The input list must not be modified.
title: Filter Active Adults by City

problem: Write a function solve(n) that takes an integer n between 1 and 3999 (inclusive) and returns a two-element list: first, the standard Roman numeral representation of n using letters I, V, X, L, C, D, M with subtractive notation (IV, IX, XL, XC, CD, CM); second, the integer value obtained by parsing that Roman numeral back using the same standard rules. The returned list must be [roman_string, parsed_integer]. The parse step must treat each numeral by scanning left to right and applying the rule that if a smaller numeral appears before a larger one, it is subtracted; otherwise it is added. n is guaranteed to be within the specified range, and the function must return the same integer n as the parsed value. Edge cases include n=1, n=4, n=9, n=40, n=90, n=400, n=900, and n=3999. Ordering is not applicable; the returned list has exactly two elements in the order specified.
title: Roman Numeral Encoder and Decoder Round Trip

problem: Given two sorted lists of integers, a and b, return a new sorted list containing the intersection of the two lists. The intersection should include each value the number of times it appears in both lists (i.e., with multiplicity). The input lists are sorted in non-decreasing order. The returned list must be sorted in non-decreasing order. If either list is empty, return an empty list. Use the two-pointer technique to achieve O(len(a) + len(b)) time. Define solve(a: list[int], b: list[int]) -> list[int].
title: Two-Pointer Intersection of Sorted Arrays

problem: Define solve(operations) where operations is a list of strings. Each string is one of: 'deposit AMOUNT', 'withdraw AMOUNT', or 'settle'. AMOUNT is a positive integer. Process operations in order using a FIFO queue (collections.deque) of pending transactions. For 'deposit' or 'withdraw', append a tuple (kind, amount) to the queue where kind is 'D' or 'W'. For 'settle', process exactly one transaction from the front of the queue if any exist; if the queue is empty, do nothing. When processing a transaction, update a balance: deposits add amount, withdrawals subtract amount. The balance starts at 0. After all operations, return a dict with keys 'balance' (final integer balance) and 'pending' (list of remaining queued transactions in FIFO order, each as [kind, amount]). If settle is called when queue is empty, queue remains empty and balance unchanged. Return exactly {'balance': int, 'pending': list of [str, int]}. Edge conditions: empty operations returns balance 0 and pending []. AMOUNT is always a positive integer with no leading zeros except '0' is not allowed. 'settle' has no amount.
title: Ledger Queue Balancer

problem: Write a function solve(a, b) that determines whether two lists of integers represent the same multiset after normalizing each list by removing all zeros and sorting the remaining non-zero values in ascending order. Return True if the normalized multisets are equal, otherwise False. The function should be pure and have no side effects. Both a and b are lists of integers (may be empty). Edge cases: empty lists, lists with only zeros, duplicate values, negative numbers, and different lengths before normalization are all possible. The comparison is based purely on the multiset of non-zero integers present in each list; the order of elements in the original lists is irrelevant.
title: Multiset Match After Normalization

problem: You are given a list of parent records for nodes in a directed forest. Each record is a tuple (child, parent). The parent may be None (or omitted) to indicate a root. From any node, following parent links eventually leads to a root or to a cycle. Implement solve(records, target) that returns the list of nodes on the unique path from the root of target's tree down to target, inclusive. If target is a root, return [target]. If target is not present in any record, return []. If following parent links from target enters a cycle (i.e., the root cannot be reached), return []. Ordering is from root to target. Records may be given in any order. There will be at most one parent per child. Use None for roots. Return an empty list if any inconsistency (e.g., duplicate child with different parents) is detected? For this exercise, assume inputs are consistent: each child appears at most once.
title: Rebuild the Family Tree Path

problem: Define a function solve(n: int, allowed_steps: list[int]) -> int that returns the number of distinct ways to climb exactly n steps using any sequence of step sizes from allowed_steps. Steps may be taken in any order, and repetition is allowed. The function must return 0 if n < 0 or if allowed_steps is empty or contains non-positive integers. Edge cases: solve(0, any_allowed_steps) returns 1 (one way: take no steps). If n=0 and allowed_steps is empty, return 0.
title: Staircase Path Counter

problem: You are given a list of sources, where each source is a list of integer timestamps sorted in non-decreasing order. Write a function solve(sources) that merges all timestamps into a single sorted list in non-decreasing order. If the same timestamp appears in multiple sources, it should appear multiple times in the result (one for each occurrence). If sources is empty or all sources are empty, return an empty list. The input sources is a list of lists of integers. The return value is a list of integers.
title: Merge Sorted Timestamps from Multiple Sources

problem: Write a function solve(records) that takes a list of dictionaries representing employee records. Each record has keys 'name' (string), 'dept' (string), and 'salary' (integer). Return a new list of these records sorted first by 'dept' in ascending alphabetical order, and then by 'salary' in descending numerical order. The sort must be stable: if two records have the same 'dept' and the same 'salary', their relative order from the input list must be preserved in the output. The function should not modify the input list. If the input list is empty, return an empty list. Signature: def solve(records): ... Return type: list of dicts.
title: Stable Sort of Employee Records by Department and Salary

problem: Define a function solve(items, discount_threshold, discount_amount) that computes the subtotal of a shopping basket. Each item is a dict with keys 'price' (integer unit price) and 'qty' (integer quantity). The subtotal is the sum of price * qty for all items. If the subtotal is greater than or equal to discount_threshold, subtract discount_amount from the subtotal. Return the final subtotal as an integer. If the basket is empty, return 0. The arguments are provided in order: items (list of dicts), discount_threshold (int), discount_amount (int). All prices, quantities, threshold, and amount are non-negative integers. The discount is applied at most once.
title: Basket Subtotal with Fixed Discount Threshold

problem: Write a function solve(n, edges) that finds all connected components of a small undirected graph with n vertices labeled 0 through n-1. The graph is given as a list of edges, where each edge is a list [u, v] representing an undirected edge between vertices u and v. Return a list of components, where each component is a list of vertex labels sorted in ascending order. The list of components must also be sorted: components are ordered by their smallest vertex (ascending). If n is 0, return an empty list. If there are no edges, each vertex is its own component. Vertices mentioned in edges must be within 0..n-1; repeated edges are allowed and ignored. solve(n, edges) takes an integer n and a list of lists of integers, and returns a list of lists of integers.
title: Find Connected Components in a Small Undirected Graph

problem: Write a function solve(expr: str) -> int that evaluates a postfix (Reverse Polish Notation) arithmetic expression containing integer literals (possibly negative) and the binary operators +, -, *, //. The expression is a space-separated string. Division is integer division with truncation toward negative infinity (floor division, consistent with Python's //). The expression is guaranteed to be valid: it contains enough operands for each operator, and no division by zero occurs. Return the integer result of evaluating the expression. Edge conditions: the expression may be a single integer with no operators; operands and operators are separated by exactly one space (but ignore leading/trailing spaces); operators are the four symbols above. Do not use eval or exec.
title: Evaluate Postfix Arithmetic

problem: Write a function solve(a, b) that returns True if list b is a cyclic permutation of list a, otherwise False. A cyclic permutation means b can be obtained by rotating a left or right by some number of positions. Both a and b are lists of integers. If lengths differ, return False. An empty list is considered a cyclic permutation of itself (return True). The comparison is exact: same elements in same relative cyclic order. Return a boolean.
title: Cyclic Permutation Validator
